method: Two disjoint random samples of the 48 body_diverged groups in reproduction.json: 12 drawn with seed 20261118, then 12 more drawn with seed 20261119 from the remaining 36 (combined n=24). Each sampled group's platform copies were diffed against the reference (skills/) copy and classified by reading the diffs: drift = divergence with no platform-specific rationale (stale or superseded copies, or edits propagated to one copy only); intentional_platform_adaptation = differing content tied to the target platform; unclear = evidence compatible with both. First-reader combined result: 21 drift, 1 intentional platform adaptation, 2 unclear; drift share 21/24 = 88% (95% Wilson interval 69-96%). These first-reader counts are superseded by the adjudicated result recorded in second_reader.adjudicated_counts (20 drift, 1 intentional platform adaptation, 3 unclear; 83%, 95% Wilson interval 64-93%), which is the result the paper reports.

reported_counts.note: The paper reports the adjudicated counts (second_reader.adjudicated_counts), not the first-reader summary_counts above.

second_reader.method: Independent second reading of the same 24 sampled groups. The reader extracted only the group names and the sampling method from this file, then classified each group from the actual diffs of every platform copy against the reference (skills/) copy in the pinned snapshot (ECC d2ef268), recording verdicts in a scratch file before opening the first reader's per-group verdicts and evidence. (The first reader's aggregate counts appear in the method string above and were visible during name extraction; the per-group verdicts were not.) Each of the 7 disagreements was then adjudicated by re-inspecting the diffs and, where relevant, corpus-wide evidence; the resolution and its basis are recorded per disagreement. The adjudicated counts below supersede summary_counts as the reported result.

verification-loop.evidence: .kiro copy is deliberately re-branded for the target platform: 'A comprehensive verification system for Kiro sessions' in description and intro (canonical: Claude Code) and Kiro-style postToolUse hook naming. It also lags canonical's pipefail hardening (a drift component), and the .agents copy is a stale pre-hardening version, but the group is the only one whose differing content is explicitly tied to the target platform.

mcp-server-patterns.basis: Genuinely ambiguous. The only body difference in both edited platform trees (.agents/.cursor) is the missing closing paragraph whose relative link (../../docs/capability-surface-selection.md) resolves only from the reference tree, which supports the first reader's deliberate-stripping reading. Against it: the pi tree retains the same paragraph although the link is equally unresolvable from pi (no pi/docs), other platform copies retain equally unresolvable ../../ links (react-patterns), and an identical absence pattern in nextjs-turbopack (a section added to the reference only) was classified drift by both readers. The diff alone cannot distinguish 'added to the reference after the platform snapshots' from 'stripped during platform edition generation'; neither reading is decisively better supported.

postgres-patterns.basis: First reader better supported. The added 'When to Use This Skill' section cannot be a leftover of an older reference text: that section appears in 0 of 314 reference-tree skills but in 10 of 43 .kiro copies, i.e. it is a .kiro-edition convention; the swapped cross-reference also points to database-migrations, a skill present in the .kiro tree, whereas the reference's target (clickhouse-io) is absent from that tree. The divergence is therefore at least partly deliberate platform-edition content, but whether it amounts to a considered platform requirement is not visible, so unclear stands.

deployment-patterns.basis: First reader better supported, on the same corpus-wide evidence as postgres-patterns: the sole body difference is the added 'When to Use This Skill' section, a section the reference tree never uses (0/314) but the .kiro edition process appends (10/43 .kiro copies). Not explicable as staleness; not demonstrably a platform requirement either.

fastapi-patterns.basis: First reader better supported. The .kiro copy is a wholesale reorganization (different heading scheme, ~2/3 the length) with no Kiro-specific content anywhere in the body. Adaptation requires positive platform-tied evidence; a rewritten edition with none falls under drift's definition (superseded copy). The bare possibility of deliberate curation is not evidence compatible with both readings.

golang-patterns.basis: First reader better supported. The .kiro copy is a heavily abridged, reorganized edition of the same pattern topics with no Kiro-specific body content. Its frontmatter carries a platform-format globs field, but that adapts the package metadata, not the diverged body being classified. No platform-specific rationale for the body divergence: drift.

python-testing.basis: First reader better supported, as for golang-patterns: an abridged alternate edition (roughly half the reference's headings) with platform-neutral pytest content; the globs frontmatter field does not explain the body divergence. Superseded/rewritten edition: drift.

verification-loop.basis: Second reader better supported. The .kiro copy was deliberately retargeted: 'A comprehensive verification system for Kiro sessions' in both description and introduction (reference: Claude Code sessions) and Kiro-style postToolUse hook naming; it is the only .kiro copy in the tree carrying such renames, and a merely stale copy cannot acquire them (the stale .agents copy still says 'Claude Code sessions'). Drift's definition requires no platform-specific rationale, which this copy demonstrably has. The copy also lags the reference's pipefail hardening, so the group is mixed, but the adaptation component is the part with a demonstrated deliberate cause.
